June. Yuki video calls Ana and Mihai from Tokyo. Next to her is a man with glasses and a shy smile: Takeshi.
Ana! Mihai! I’m calling so you’re the first to know: Takeshi and I are engaged!
Oh, Yuki! Congratulations! How did he propose?
Nice to meet you. Well… as Yuki is always talking about the cherry trees in Kyoto, I proposed there, in April, under a cherry tree in blossom.
How romantic! You speak very good Spanish, Takeshi.
Thank you. I’m a Spanish teacher. Although Yuki says I talk like a book, because I learned in Salamanca.
It’s true. And I talk like someone from Madrid, thanks to you two. That’s exactly how we met.
Because of your accent?
Not because of, thanks to my accent! At a meeting at the university I said “vale, tío”, and he corrected me in front of everyone.
While we’re telling the truth: I went very red. I apologised the next day, with a coffee. And that’s how it all started.
And when’s the wedding?
In October, at a shrine in Kyoto. Given that his parents are elderly, we don’t want them to travel. It’ll be a traditional ceremony, with kimonos.
And can we come? Please say yes!
Of course! That’s exactly why I’m calling: so you can book your tickets early. I want the whole club to come. And Rosa Elena has to carry the flowers.
Then we’re coming. Even if we have to sell the car to pay for the trip.
That won’t be necessary. Because of the wedding, my family has rented a huge house in Kyoto. There’s room for everyone.

1. Cause: porque, como, ya que, dado que
Position
Register
after the main clause
neutral

ALWAYS at the start

Causal “como” goes at the START. You can’t say “No vino como estaba enfermo”. And “porque” doesn’t usually go at the start of a statement: the correct form is “Como llovía, no salimos”.
2. Gracias a vs. por culpa de
Both mean “because of”, but they show what you think of the cause:
gracias a (positive)
por culpa de (negative)
Aprobé gracias a mi profesora.
Suspendí por culpa de los nervios.
Nos conocimos gracias a un acento.
Perdimos el tren por culpa de la lluvia.

It’s like English “thanks to” (good) versus “because of / it’s the … fault” (bad). Don’t say “gracias a la lluvia” for something bad, just as you wouldn’t say “thanks to the rain, we missed the train”!
3. Por + infinitive: the cause of an action
“Por + infinitive” explains why something happened to someone. For the past, use “por + haber + participle”:
They congratulated him for winning the competition.
He talks like a book because he learned in Salamanca.
Very common with verbs of thanking, apologising and praising: Gracias por venir. Perdón por llegar tarde. Te felicito por aprobar.

Review from chapter 40: “para que” is ALWAYS followed by the subjunctive. In the past, the imperfect subjunctive: Os llamé para que lo supierais.
Don’t confuse: “para” (purpose, in order to) and “por” (cause, because of). Estudio para aprobar (purpose) / Aprobé por estudiar (cause).

Cómo se conocieron Yuki y Takeshi

Takeshi Mori was the most serious lecturer in the Spanish department at the University of Tokyo. He always wore a tie, even in August. He marked papers in green ink, because he said red was aggressive. And he spoke such perfect Spanish that the students laughed at him behind his back.

He had learned Spanish in Salamanca, at twenty, living with a family of retired teachers who read nothing but Cervantes. Because he had lived with them, he said things like “menester”, “acaso” and “heme aquí”. Nobody in Tokyo talked like that. Not even in Spain.

Yuki joined the department in September, after five years in Madrid. She was the exact opposite: she wore jeans, laughed very loudly and talked like someone from Lavapiés. She said “vale” every three words, “tío” to everyone and “flipo” when something surprised her.

As they both taught Spanish, they had to share an office. At first they barely spoke. Takeshi greeted her with a very formal bow of the head. Yuki answered with a “Hi, Takeshi, mate! How’s it going?” that made him blush to the tips of his ears.
The incident happened in October, at the department’s first meeting. The head asked if anyone had any suggestions for the academic year. Yuki raised her hand and said:
“OK, mate, I’ve got a super cool idea (“mola mazo”): why don’t we start a Spanish club, like the one at the library in Madrid?”
There was silence. The Japanese lecturers, who didn’t understand the register, nodded politely. But Takeshi, at the back of the room, raised his hand too.

“With all due respect,” he said in his calm voice, “Miss Tanaka should know that ‘mola mazo’ is not an appropriate expression for an academic meeting. Owing to our responsibility as teachers, we should set an example.”
Yuki was left open-mouthed. Nobody had corrected her like that in public since she was ten. She felt her face go red, not with embarrassment but with fury.

“Thank you for the correction, Mr Mori,” she answered, with a frozen smile. “But given that we’ll be teaching twenty-first-century Spanish, perhaps we should use twenty-first-century Spanish. Not Don Quixote’s.”
A few lecturers laughed. The head coughed. The meeting went on, but the atmosphere in the shared office became arctic.

The next day, when Yuki got to the office, there was a coffee on her desk. A white coffee, with lots of milk and half a teaspoon of sugar, exactly the way she liked it. Next to it, a note written in green ink:
“Miss Tanaka: I apologise for yesterday’s comment. You were right. Perhaps it is menester (necessary) for me to learn today’s Spanish. Would you teach it to me? Takeshi.”
Yuki read the note three times. Then she burst out laughing, so loudly that the secretary in the corridor poked her head round the door to see what was going on.
“How did you know how I like my coffee?” she asked Takeshi when he came in.
He went red again. “Because I’ve been watching you for a month. You order the same thing every morning at the café. I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to seem… strange.”

That’s how the secret lessons began. Every afternoon after work, Yuki taught Takeshi street Spanish. Thanks to her, he learned to say “vale”, “guay” and “qué fuerte”. Thanks to him, she learned that “menester” is a beautiful word and that the subjunctive has an elegance she had never noticed.
To practise, they started watching Spanish films together. First in the office. Then at the cinema. Then in Takeshi’s flat, where he had a huge collection of Almodóvar films that nobody knew about.

One day in December, watching “Volver”, Takeshi said “¡qué fuerte!” without realising it. Yuki looked at him, surprised. He covered his mouth with his hand. And they both laughed until their stomachs hurt.
That night Yuki realised she had fallen in love. Because of an accent. Or thanks to one. She never managed to decide which of the two expressions was the right one.
In April, Takeshi invited her to Kyoto, to see the cherry blossoms at the shrine where his grandparents had married. He was wearing a tie, as usual. But this time his hands were shaking.

Under the oldest cherry tree, he knelt down on the stones. He took a little box out of his pocket. And instead of saying it in Japanese, he said it in Spanish. But not in the Spanish of Salamanca, or of books.
“Yuki, love… will you marry me? It’d be super cool.”
Yuki laughed and cried at the same time. Then she answered him in the most elegant Spanish she knew, with a perfect subjunctive:
“Yes, I will. Provided you keep bringing me my coffee every morning.”

When Yuki finished telling the story, on the video call with Bucharest, Ana’s eyes were full of tears. Mihai was smiling. And Rosa Elena, who hadn’t understood a thing, was clapping because the grown-ups seemed happy.
“Yuki,” said Ana, “do you realise? You taught Mihai and me Spanish at a club. And now Spanish has led you to the love of your life.”
“I know,” Yuki answered. “That’s why I want the wedding to be half Japanese and half Spanish. So that Spanish is there too. Like one more guest.”
Takeshi, next to her, nodded very seriously. Then, unable to help himself, he added: “It’s super cool.”

Ana laughed so loudly she woke the neighbour. Mrs Maria looked over the fence in her nightdress and asked what was going on. Mihai explained to her, in Romanian, that a Japanese woman and a Japanese man were getting married thanks to a Madrid accent. Mrs Maria thought for a moment, shrugged and said that could have happened in Romania too.

In the following weeks, the house in the old neighbourhood turned into a travel agency. Ana was looking for cheap flights. Mihai was asking for leave at the hospital. Elena, who had decided to come too “to look after the baby”, was knitting a woollen kimono for Rosa Elena, although nobody had explained to her that kimonos aren’t knitted.

Rosa Elena, for her part, took her role very seriously. As she was going to carry the flowers, she practised every afternoon in the yard with a bunch of daisies Mrs Maria gave her. She walked very slowly, very seriously, looking straight ahead, followed by the neighbour’s six cats, who looked like her bridesmaids.
One day, halfway through the rehearsal, she tripped and fell. The daisies flew through the air. The cats ran off. Ana rushed over, thinking she was going to burst into tears.
But Rosa Elena didn’t cry. She got up by herself, picked up the flowers one by one and said, very dignified, in her mix of three languages: “Otra vez. Încă o dată. Mō ichido.”
Mihai, who had seen everything from the balcony, said quietly to Ana: “She takes after you. However many times she falls, she gets back up.”

“No,” Ana answered, smiling. “She takes after everyone. Your grandfather, who waited in the snow. My grandmother, who waited a month shut in at home. Yuki, who fell in love with someone who had corrected her in front of everyone.”
That evening, Ana sent Yuki a short message: “Your flower girl is ready. Well, almost. Get ready for a very serious little girl with six imaginary cats behind her.”
